summaries.summary: NMT has gained popularity, with Cho2014's encoder-decoder using two RNNs and DzmitryBahdana2014's attention-based NMT improving translation adequacy.
Open NMT questions include over-translation and under-translation, attributed by Tu2016, Mi2016a, and Feng2016 to incomplete source information transfer and lacking coverage vector.
NMT's cross-entropy objective does not directly maximize translation accuracy, while Shen2016's expected BLEU optimization improved accuracy but BLEU may permit word repetition.
tu2016neural introduced an encoder-decoder-reconstructor framework using back-translation from output sentences into original source sentences to address repeating and missing words.
Experiments on English-Japanese and Japanese-English parallel corpora show significant BLEU improvement and fewer repeating and missing words for English-Japanese, but not Japanese-English.
Jointly training forward translation and back-translation without pre-training fails, proving forward translation pre-training similar to conventional attention-based NMT is required.
The main contributions of this paper are as follows.
Prior NMT studies addressed missing or repeating words using PBSMT outputs or coverage vector, while this method uses back-translation and needs no additional testing parameters.
Meng2016 and Feng2016 attention mechanisms indirectly reduce over-translation, whereas this work directly penalizes translation mismatch by considering back-translation.
tu2016neural's encoder-decoder-reconstructor optimizes NMT by reconstructor using back-translation and significantly improves BLEU scores on a Chinese-English translation task.
The attention-based NMT proposed by DzmitryBahdana2014 is described as shown in Figure FIGREF1.
The encoder converts the input sequence INLINEFORM0 into a fixed-length vector using an RNN, with hidden state INLINEFORM2 at time step INLINEFORM1.
A bidirectional RNN computes the forward state INLINEFORM0 and backward state INLINEFORM1 by DISPLAYFORM0.

INLINEFORM0 and INLINEFORM1 are nonlinear functions, and hidden states INLINEFORM2 are converted into fixed-length vector INLINEFORM3 as DISPLAYFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 is a nonlinear function.
The decoder converts fixed-length vector INLINEFORM0 into target sequence INLINEFORM1 using an RNN, computing output word INLINEFORM3 probability at time step INLINEFORM2.
INLINEFORM0 is a nonlinear function, and decoder hidden state INLINEFORM1 is presented as DISPLAYFORM0.
The decoder hidden state uses previous hidden state INLINEFORM0, previous target word INLINEFORM1, and context vector INLINEFORM2.
Context vector INLINEFORM0 is a weighted sum of each encoder hidden state INLINEFORM1 and is presented as DISPLAYFORM0.
Weight INLINEFORM0 is a normalized probability distribution computed by DISPLAYFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 is a weight vector, and INLINEFORM1 and INLINEFORM2 are weight matrices.
The objective function is defined by DISPLAYFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 is the number of data, and INLINEFORM1 is a model parameter.
The hyperbolic tangent function or the rectified linear unit are generally used as nonlinear functions.
The encoder-decoder-reconstructor framework combines standard attention-based NMT by DzmitryBahdana2014 with a reconstructor back-translating decoder hidden states to the source sentence.
The reconstructor back-translates decoder hidden state into source sequence INLINEFORM0, computing output word INLINEFORM2 probability at time step INLINEFORM1 by DISPLAYFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 is a nonlinear function, and reconstructor hidden state INLINEFORM1 is presented as DISPLAYFORM0.
The reconstructor hidden state uses previous hidden state INLINEFORM0, previous source word INLINEFORM1, and inverse context vector INLINEFORM2.
Inverse context vector INLINEFORM0 is a weighted sum of each decoder hidden state INLINEFORM1 on forward translation and is presented as DISPLAYFORM0.
INLINEFORM0 is the number of data, INLINEFORM1 and INLINEFORM2 are model parameters, and INLINEFORM3 weights forward translation and back-translation.
The objective function has forward measuring translation fluency and backward measuring translation adequacy, better guiding parameter training for overall translation quality.
The encoder-decoder-reconstructor is trained with likelihood of both encoder-decoder and reconstructor, with tu2016neural training back-translation after forward translation pre-training.
The authors experiment with jointly training forward translation and back-translation without pre-training, which may learn a globally optimal model.
tu2016neural used beam search on testing, but this paper does not use beam search for simplicity and effectiveness.
The encoder-decoder-reconstructor framework for NMT was evaluated on English-Japanese and Japanese-English translation tasks.
Two parallel corpora, ASPEC and NTCIR PatentMT Parallel Corpus, were used, with ASPEC training data limited to the first 1 million sentences and sentences with more than 40 words excluded.

Models included baseline-NMT, encoder-decoder-reconstructor, and jointly trained encoder-decoder-reconstructor without pre-training, with RNN settings of 512 hidden units, 512 embedding units, 30,000 vocabulary size, and 64 batch size.
The encoder-decoder-reconstructor significantly improves BLEU by 1.01 points on ASPEC and 1.37 points on NTCIR in English-Japanese translation, but not Japanese-English.
Table TABREF24 shows English-Japanese examples where encoder-decoder-reconstructor restores missing text and avoids repeated “UTF8min新生児” and “UTF8min30歳以上の” outputs.
Figures FIGREF25 and FIGREF25 show baseline-NMT attention errors and repeated attention, while encoder-decoder-reconstructor attention almost correctly attends input words.
Table TABREF28 shows reduced redundant word occurrences in all cases, confirming encoder-decoder-reconstructor reduces repeating and missing words while maintaining translation quality.
The encoder-decoder-reconstructor significantly improves BLEU scores and alleviates repeating and missing words on English-Japanese translation, and cannot be trained well without pre-training.
